newsitem.title: USA: Jan NAPM drops, hints U.S. manufacturing slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Jan NAPM drops, hints U.S. manufacturing slowdown.

text.p: The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index dropped more than expected in January, suggesting the U.S. manufacturing sector will likely slow down in the first quarter, analysts said.

"(The report) signals that maybe the manufacturing strength will slow down early this year. We're going to get some more tempered type of numbers," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
The January NAPM index was 52.0 against a revised reading of 53.8 in December. Wall Street economists in a Reuters poll had expected the indicator to post a 53.0 reading in January.
A reading above 50 is usually seen by analysts as an indication of strength in the manufacturing sector.
But the declining curve the index projected this month made some experts believe the sector's strength posted in the fourth quarter of 1996 might be waning.
Despite a small rise in NAPM's prices index in January to 51.4, analysts said they detected no signs of inflationary pressures emanating from the manufacturing sector.
"The numbers signal very few price pressures from the factory sector ... It seems to imply that price pressures will be somewhat limited," Strauss said.

Pundits said the NAPM report was expected to have a positive impact on financial markets. "It's a positive report for the markets ... What's wrong with a little bit stronger growth if we don't have the price pressures?" Strauss said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond erased early losses to gain almost half a point to 96-25/32 shortly after the index was released at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
"The (bond) market liked the number. It shows the economy might not be as strong as we thought after all," said the head of the Treasury desk at a major U.S. investment bank.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved higher from lows and then fell further after the NAPM index was released. At 1115 EST/1615 the Dow was off 28.1 points at 6784 points.
Analysts said the NAPM report also showed industry inventories remained controlled, with no signs of inflationary pressures.
"Things are not overheating here by any means. Inventories remained extraordinarily well-contained," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.

Inventories showed a reading of 44.4 in January against 44.9 in the previous month. A strong drop in new orders to 53.5 from 58.2 was also seen as another indication that the manufacturing sector might be slowing.

Analysts were a little wary, however, about a rise in the employment index in January to 48.7 from 47.5 in December. Such a jump, they said, might put some upward pressure in the January non-farm payrolls report due out on Friday.
"Near term it does point to some strength in factory employment for this Friday's employment number," Sanwa's chief economist Strauss said. "That was the only negative I could find in the report."
Analysts in a Reuters survey expect January non-farm payrolls to rise by 347,000 jobs against a 355,000 jump in the previous month.
